before.description: How media products reach audiences through online, physical, and broadcast distribution platforms.
before.content_html:
What Are Distribution Platforms?

Distribution refers to the methods used to deliver media products to their target audience. Once a media product has been created in the production and post-production stages, it needs to reach the people it was designed for. The platform chosen for distribution affects the file format, quality, and accessibility of the final product.

The OCR specification identifies three main categories of distribution: online platforms, physical platforms, and physical media. Each has distinct characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages that media professionals must consider when deciding how to deliver their work.

Key Fact

The three categories of distribution are: online (apps, multimedia, web), physical platforms (computers, interactive TV, kiosks, mobile devices), and physical media (CD/DVD, memory sticks, paper-based).

Online Distribution

Online distribution delivers media products through the internet. This is the most common method of distribution in the modern media industry. Online distribution includes:

Apps — mobile applications downloaded from app stores (Google Play, Apple App Store). These can deliver games, music, video, and interactive content directly to smartphones and tablets. Apps like Spotify, Netflix, and TikTok are examples of media products distributed this way.

Websites — content accessed through web browsers. Websites can host video, audio, images, animations, and text. Examples include YouTube, BBC iPlayer, and online news sites. Websites are accessible on any device with a browser and internet connection.

Multimedia — platforms that combine multiple media types (text, images, audio, video, animation) and deliver them online. Streaming services, social media platforms, and e-learning sites are all multimedia distribution channels.

Advantages: Widespread reach — anyone with internet access can view the content. Cheap to distribute compared to producing physical copies. Content can be updated instantly without reprinting or re-manufacturing. Products are available immediately without waiting for delivery.

Disadvantages: Requires internet access, which not everyone has reliably. Security risks such as piracy, hacking, and unauthorised copying. Competition is fierce because the barrier to entry is low — thousands of similar products are available online. Some users may experience buffering or slow loading if their connection is poor.

Physical Platforms

Physical platforms are the actual devices used to play or show media products. They are not the media itself, but the hardware that displays it. The specification identifies four types:

Computers — desktops and laptops can display websites, play video, run software applications, and show digital graphics. They support a wide range of file formats and offer high-resolution displays.

Interactive TV — digital television services that allow viewers to interact with content, such as pressing the red button for extra features, voting on shows, or accessing catch-up services. Freeview, Sky, and Virgin Media all offer interactive features.

Kiosks — standalone touchscreen terminals found in public spaces such as shopping centres, restaurants, airports, and museums. They deliver information, allow ordering, or provide entertainment. McDonald’s ordering kiosks and museum information points are common examples.

Mobile devices — smartphones and tablets that can display media products on the move. They support apps, websites, video, audio, and games. Mobile devices are the most widely used platform for consuming media — over 60% of global internet traffic now comes from mobile devices.

Key Fact

Physical platforms are the devices (computers, interactive TV, kiosks, mobile devices) that display media. Physical media are the storage formats (CD, DVD, memory stick, paper) that carry the content. Do not confuse the two in the exam.

Physical Media

Physical media are tangible items that store media products and can be given to the audience. Unlike online distribution, physical media must be manufactured and physically delivered.

CD/DVD — optical discs that store audio, video, software, and data. CDs hold up to 700 MB, while DVDs can store 4.7 GB (single layer) or 8.5 GB (dual layer). Blu-ray discs offer even higher capacity at 25 GB or 50 GB. Although declining in popularity, DVDs and Blu-rays are still used for film distribution and software installation.

Memory sticks (USB flash drives) — portable storage devices that can hold files of various types. Useful for transferring files between devices or distributing software, presentations, and digital portfolios. Capacities typically range from 8 GB to 256 GB.

Paper-based — printed materials such as newspapers, magazines, leaflets, brochures, posters, and flyers. Despite the growth of digital media, paper-based distribution remains important for local advertising, event promotion, and some publishing.

Advantages: The audience has a physical copy to refer back to at any time without needing internet access. Can deliver a clear, focused message (e.g. a printed leaflet at an event). Content is private — only the person with the disc or printout has access. No risk of buffering or connectivity issues.

Disadvantages: Can be lost, damaged, or scratched. Higher production and distribution costs (manufacturing, printing, postage). Not as widespread — you can only reach people who physically receive the item. Cannot be updated once produced — mistakes or changes require a new print run. Environmental impact of manufacturing and disposal.

How Platform Choice Affects File Formats

The distribution platform directly affects which file formats a media professional should use for the final product. A video intended for streaming on a website needs to be compressed into a format like MP4 that loads quickly, even on slower connections. A video for a Blu-ray disc can use higher quality, less compressed formats because the disc has more storage capacity and the player can handle larger files.

Images for a website should be saved as JPEG or PNG at 72 DPI to keep file sizes small and loading times fast. Images for a printed leaflet need to be at least 300 DPI in a format like TIFF or high-quality PDF to ensure sharp printing. Audio for streaming uses compressed formats like MP3 or AAC, while audio for a CD uses uncompressed WAV at 44,100 Hz sample rate.

A music festival wants to promote its event. For online distribution, the organisers create a website with embedded video trailers (MP4 format, compressed), social media posts with JPEG images, and a Spotify playlist. For physical platforms, they set up interactive kiosks at the venue showing maps and schedules. For physical media, they print A5 leaflets and posters for local shops and hand out USB drives with press packs at media events. Each platform requires different file formats and quality levels to work effectively.

Key Fact

The exam may give you a scenario and ask you to explain which distribution platform is most suitable. Always consider the target audience, the type of product, and the advantages/disadvantages of each platform when answering.
before.exam_tip_html: In the R093 exam, questions on distribution platforms often appear in Section B with a scenario. You might be asked to explain an advantage of using an online platform for the audience or for the distributor — read the question carefully to know whose perspective to write from. For 2-mark “Explain” questions, always give a reason and a developed consequence (e.g. “They won’t need to wait for delivery (1), meaning they can access it immediately (1)”).

1 marks for each valid example (max 2):

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a physical platform and physical media.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• A physical platform is a device used to play or show media products (1), such as a computer or interactive TV (1).
• Physical media are tangible storage formats used to store and distribute products (1), such as CDs, DVDs, or memory sticks (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage for the audience of using an online platform rather than physical media to access a video.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for a developed explanation:
• They won’t need to wait for a disc to be delivered / spend time going to the shops (1), meaning they can watch the video immediately (1).
• They won’t need to store a physical disc (1), reducing the amount of physical storage space needed in their home (1).
• The video will be streamed on apps or websites which users are likely to already have access to (1), without needing a DVD/Blu-ray player (1).
• Accept other valid advantages with development.

practice_questions.text: A local charity wants to promote an upcoming fundraising event. Explain why the charity might choose to use paper-based distribution rather than online distribution.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation with clear reasoning and examples.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation with some reasoning.
Lower band (1-2): Basic explanation.
Indicative content:
• The charity’s target audience may be local residents who would respond well to leaflets posted through doors or displayed in community centres
• Paper-based materials like posters can be placed in physical locations where the target audience will see them (shops, notice boards)
• Not all target audience members may have reliable internet access, especially older demographics
• A printed leaflet gives the reader something tangible to keep and refer to for event details
• However, paper-based distribution has higher costs (printing, delivery) and cannot be updated once printed
• The reach is limited to the local area which may be appropriate for a local event

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using online distribution compared to physical media for a new music album release.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both sides with clear analysis and a conclusion. QWC: specialist terminology used accurately.
Mid band (4-6): Sound discussion covering both advantages and disadvantages.
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited development.
Indicative content:
Online advantages:
• Widespread reach — anyone with internet can access it globally
• Lower cost — no manufacturing or shipping of physical discs
• Immediate availability — released simultaneously worldwide
• Can be updated or patched after release
Physical media advantages:
• Collectors value physical copies (vinyl, CD) as tangible products
• No internet required to play
• Higher audio quality possible (e.g. uncompressed WAV on CD vs compressed MP3 streaming)
• Cannot be lost to server outages or licensing changes
Conclusion should weigh target audience preferences, costs, and the artist’s goals.

before.description: Pixels, resolution, DPI vs PPI, colour depth, bitmap vs vector, and image file formats explained.
before.content_html:
Properties of Digital Image Files

Every digital image is made up of tiny coloured squares called pixels. The more pixels an image contains, the more detail it can show. Understanding the properties of image files — resolution, pixel dimensions, and colour depth — is essential for choosing the right format and quality settings for different uses.

Resolution: DPI and PPI

Resolution describes how much detail an image contains. It is measured in two ways depending on whether the image is displayed on screen or printed on paper.

PPI (Pixels Per Inch) refers to the number of pixels contained within one inch of an image displayed on a computer monitor or screen. A higher PPI means more pixels are packed into each inch, producing a sharper, more detailed image on screen.

DPI (Dots Per Inch) refers to the number of printed dots contained within one inch of an image printed by a printer. A higher DPI produces a clearer printed image with smoother gradients and finer detail.

Key Fact

PPI is for screens, DPI is for printing. Web images typically use 72 PPI. Print images need at least 300 DPI for sharp, professional-quality output.

Pixel dimensions describe the width and height of an image in pixels (e.g. 1920 × 1080). Larger pixel dimensions mean more detail, but also a larger file size. An image with dimensions of 3000 × 2000 pixels contains 6 million pixels (6 megapixels). If you enlarge a bitmap image beyond its original pixel dimensions, it becomes blurry or “pixelated” because the existing pixels are stretched to fill a larger area.

Bitmap (Raster) vs Vector Images

Digital images fall into two fundamental categories: bitmap (also called raster) and vector. Understanding the difference is critical for choosing the right format.

A bitmap (or raster) image is made up of a grid of pixels. Each pixel stores colour information. Photographs are always bitmap images. File sizes tend to be larger because every pixel must be stored. If a bitmap image is enlarged, it becomes blurry and pixelated because the pixels are stretched. Common bitmap formats include JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF, and BMP.

A vector image is made up of mathematical shapes — lines, curves, and fills defined by coordinates and equations. Vector images can be scaled to any size without losing quality, because the shapes are recalculated at each new size rather than stretched. File sizes are generally smaller than bitmaps. Vector images are ideal for logos, icons, diagrams, and illustrations. Common vector formats include SVG and PDF.

Bitmap: Made of pixels. Best for photographs. Large file sizes. Loses quality when enlarged. Formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF, BMP.

Vector: Made of mathematical shapes. Best for logos, icons, illustrations. Small file sizes. Scales without quality loss. Formats: SVG, PDF, EPS.

Image File Formats

Different image file formats have different properties that make them suitable for specific uses. The exam requires you to know the properties and limitations of each format and when to use them.

JPEG (.jpg) — Bitmap format using lossy compression. Reduces file size by permanently removing some image data. Best for photographs and web images where small file size matters. Standard web resolution is 72 PPI. Does not support transparency. Every time a JPEG is edited and re-saved, quality decreases slightly.

PNG (.png) — Bitmap format using lossless compression. Preserves all image data while reducing file size. Supports transparency (alpha channel), making it ideal for logos and web graphics that need to appear on different backgrounds. File sizes are slightly larger than JPEG. Standard web resolution is 96 PPI.

GIF (.gif) — Bitmap format using lossless compression. Limited to 256 colours, making it unsuitable for photographs but useful for simple graphics and short animations. Supports transparency and frame-based animation. Very small file sizes.

TIFF (.tiff) — Bitmap format that is typically uncompressed (though it can use lossless compression). Produces very high-quality images at 300 DPI, making it the standard format for professional printing. File sizes are very large. Not suitable for web use.

BMP (.bmp) — The standard uncompressed bitmap format. Very high quality but produces extremely large file sizes. Rarely used for distribution; mainly used in image editing software.

SVG (.svg) — A vector format that uses mathematical definitions rather than pixels. Scalable to any size without quality loss. Ideal for logos, icons, web illustrations, and diagrams. Small file sizes. Supported by all modern web browsers.

RAW — An unprocessed image file captured directly from a digital camera sensor. Contains maximum image data for editing flexibility. Very large file sizes. Must be processed and exported to another format (JPEG, TIFF) before distribution. RAW is a native format — different cameras use different RAW formats (e.g. .dng, .nef, .cr2).

File Compression for Images

File compression reduces the size of image files so they can be stored and transferred more efficiently. There are two types of compression:

Lossy compression permanently removes some data to reduce file size. The removed data cannot be recovered. Each time the file is edited and re-saved, more data is lost and quality decreases further. JPEG is the most common lossy format. Lossy compression is best when small file sizes matter more than perfect quality (e.g. web images, social media posts).

Lossless compression reduces file size without permanently removing any data. The original image can be perfectly reconstructed from the compressed file. PNG, GIF, and TIFF (when compressed) all use lossless compression. Lossless compression produces larger files than lossy but maintains full image quality.

Key Fact

Lossy = smaller file, some quality lost permanently (JPEG). Lossless = larger file, no quality lost (PNG, GIF). The choice depends on whether file size or image quality is the priority.

Native file formats can only be opened by specific software. Examples: Adobe Photoshop (.psd), Adobe Illustrator (.ai), Affinity Designer (.afdesign), GIMP (.xcf), RAW camera files. These are used during editing and must be exported to a standard format for distribution.

Standard file formats can be opened without specialist software and are used for final products. Examples: JPEG, PNG, GIF, TIFF, SVG, PDF, BMP.
before.exam_tip_html: A common exam question asks: “What type of images maintain exactly the same quality regardless of how much the image size is increased?” The answer is vector images (not bitmap/raster). Remember: bitmaps pixelate when enlarged, vectors scale perfectly. For questions about choosing file formats, always link your answer to the use and context — state the format, explain why it suits the purpose (e.g. “JPEG for a website because its lossy compression keeps the file size small for fast loading”).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression for image files.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Lossy compression permanently removes some data to reduce file size (1)
• Lossless compression reduces file size without removing any data (1)

practice_questions.text: Some images maintain exactly the same quality regardless of how much the image size is increased. What type of images are these? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Vector images (1)
• Vector images are made up of mathematical shapes/lines/curves (1)
• When the image is resized, the shapes are recalculated at the new size (1)
• So no detail or quality is lost regardless of how large the image is made (1)
• Do not accept: raster, bitmap, or compressed images.

practice_questions.text: A graphic designer needs to create a company logo that will be used on business cards, a website, and a large billboard. Explain why a vector file format would be more suitable than a bitmap format for this task.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation with clear reasoning linked to the scenario.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation with some development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points.
Indicative content:
• The logo needs to be used at very different sizes (small on business cards, large on billboard)
• Vector images can be scaled to any size without losing quality because they use mathematical shapes
• A bitmap would pixelate when enlarged to billboard size, looking blurry and unprofessional
• Vector files are generally smaller in size, making them easier to share and store
• Vector formats like SVG are supported by web browsers for the website version
• The logo can be exported from the vector to bitmap formats (JPEG, PNG) for specific uses while keeping the master file as vector

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether JPEG or PNG is the better file format for images on a website.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion covering both formats with a reasoned conclusion. QWC: specialist terminology used accurately.
Mid band (4-6): Sound discussion of both formats.
Lower band (1-3): Basic comparison.
Indicative content:
JPEG advantages:
• Smaller file sizes due to lossy compression, meaning faster page loading
• Widely supported across all browsers and devices
• Best for photographs and images with many colours
JPEG disadvantages:
• Does not support transparency
• Quality degrades each time the file is re-saved
PNG advantages:
• Supports transparency (alpha channel) — essential for logos on varied backgrounds
• Lossless compression preserves full quality
• Can be re-saved without quality loss
PNG disadvantages:
• Larger file sizes than JPEG
• Not as efficient for photographs with millions of colours
Conclusion: depends on use — JPEG for photos, PNG for logos and graphics needing transparency.

flashcard_questions.q: The smallest individual unit of a digital image, displayed as a tiny coloured square on screen.
Pixels Per Inch — the number of pixels contained within one inch of an image displayed on a screen.
Dots Per Inch — the number of printed dots contained within one inch of an image produced by a printer.

before.content_html:
How Digital Audio Works

Sound travels through the air as analogue sound waves. When we want to store or distribute sound using a computer, the analogue signal must be converted into a digital format that the computer can understand. This process is called digital sampling.

Sampling works by measuring the sound wave at regular intervals — taking thousands of tiny “snapshots” of the sound every second. Each snapshot records the amplitude (loudness) of the wave at that exact moment. When these snapshots are played back in sequence, they recreate the original sound.

Key Fact

The two key properties of digital audio are sample rate (how many times per second the sound is measured) and bit depth (how accurately each measurement is recorded). Higher values of both mean higher quality sound — but also larger file sizes.

Sample Rate

Sample rate is the number of times per second that the sound wave is measured. It is expressed in Hertz (Hz). A sample rate of 44,100 Hz (often written as 44.1 kHz) means the sound wave is sampled 44,100 times every second.

The higher the sample rate, the more accurately the digital version captures the original analogue sound. Common sample rates include:

22,050 Hz (22.05 kHz) — lower quality, suitable for speech recordings and podcasts where file size needs to be small. 44,100 Hz (44.1 kHz) — CD quality, the standard for music distribution. This is the most commonly referenced sample rate in the exam. 48,000 Hz (48 kHz) — used in professional video production and broadcast audio. 96,000 Hz (96 kHz) — high-resolution audio for professional studio recording.

Human hearing can detect frequencies up to about 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). To accurately capture all audible frequencies, the sample rate must be at least double the highest frequency — this is known as the Nyquist theorem. Double 20,000 Hz gives 40,000 Hz as the minimum. The standard of 44,100 Hz provides a small safety margin above this minimum, ensuring all audible sound is captured faithfully.

Bit Depth

Bit depth determines how accurately each individual sample is recorded. It measures how many possible amplitude values each sample can represent. Think of it as the “detail” of each snapshot.

An 8-bit recording can represent 256 different amplitude levels. A 16-bit recording (CD quality) can represent 65,536 levels, capturing far more subtle variations in volume. A 24-bit recording (professional studio quality) offers over 16.7 million levels. The higher the bit depth, the more faithfully the digital file captures quiet sounds, subtle dynamics, and the full range of the original recording.

Key Fact

CD-quality audio uses a sample rate of 44,100 Hz and a bit depth of 16 bits. Remember: sample rate = how often, bit depth = how detailed.

Channels: Mono and Stereo

Channels refer to the number of separate audio tracks in a recording. Mono audio has one channel — the same sound plays through all speakers. Stereo audio has two channels (left and right), allowing different sounds to be directed to different speakers for a more immersive listening experience. Stereo files are roughly double the size of mono files because they contain twice the data.

Audio File Formats

Audio file formats fall into three categories: uncompressed, lossless compressed, and lossy compressed. Each has different properties that suit different purposes.

WAV (.wav) — Waveform Audio File. Excellent sound quality with no compression at all. Widely supported across all editing software and operating systems. Standard for audio editing and production. However, file sizes are very large (a 3-minute song at CD quality is approximately 30 MB), making WAV unsuitable for streaming or limited storage.

AIFF (.aiff) — Audio Interchange File Format. Apple’s equivalent of WAV. High quality, uncompressed, widely used in professional audio on Mac systems. Large file sizes, and less common outside the Apple ecosystem.

MP3 (.mp3) — The most popular lossy audio format. Reduces file size significantly (typically to about one-tenth of the uncompressed size) by removing audio data that most listeners cannot hear. Widely supported on virtually all devices and platforms. Ideal for music streaming and downloads. Limitation: some sound quality is permanently lost, especially at very low bitrates.

AAC (.aac) — Advanced Audio Coding. Produces better sound quality than MP3 at the same file size. Used by Apple (iTunes, Apple Music), YouTube, and many streaming services. Limitation: not as universally supported as MP3 on older devices.

OGG Vorbis (.ogg) — An open-source lossy format with good quality at small file sizes. No licensing fees, unlike MP3. Used in some games and open-source software. Limitation: limited support on some mainstream devices and music players.

FLAC (.flac) — Free Lossless Audio Codec. Compresses audio to about half the size of WAV while preserving 100% of the original quality. Open-source with no licensing fees. Widely supported on most modern devices and music players. Limitation: larger file sizes than MP3/AAC, and not supported on all older devices (particularly some Apple products).

ALAC (.m4a) — Apple Lossless Audio Codec. Apple’s equivalent of FLAC. Works seamlessly with iTunes and Apple devices. Full quality preservation with moderate file sizes. Limitation: mainly used within the Apple ecosystem.

Key Fact

Uncompressed (WAV, AIFF) = best quality, largest files, used for editing. Lossy (MP3, AAC, OGG) = small files, some quality lost, used for streaming and sharing. Lossless (FLAC, ALAC) = full quality preserved, moderate file sizes, used by audiophiles.

Choosing the Right Audio Format

The right format depends on the intended use. For streaming and downloads, MP3 or AAC is preferred because small file sizes allow fast loading and minimal data usage. For CD distribution, uncompressed WAV at 44.1 kHz / 16-bit is the standard. For professional editing, WAV or AIFF preserves full quality during production. For archiving, FLAC offers a good balance of quality preservation and reduced storage space.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Lossy compression permanently removes some audio data to reduce file size (1)
• Lossless compression reduces file size without removing any data (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why a music producer would use WAV format during the editing stage but export the final track as MP3 for streaming.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• WAV is uncompressed so it retains full audio quality during editing (1)
• This means no data is lost when making edits, cuts, or applying effects (1)

practice_questions.text: A podcast creator needs to choose between recording at 22,050 Hz and 44,100 Hz sample rate. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of choosing the higher sample rate.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation with developed reasoning for both advantage and disadvantage.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation of both sides.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points.
Indicative content:
Advantage of 44,100 Hz:
• The sound wave is sampled more frequently, capturing more detail
• This produces a higher quality recording that sounds closer to the original
• If the podcast includes music or sound effects, the higher sample rate preserves audio fidelity
Disadvantage of 44,100 Hz:
• The file size will be significantly larger because more data is captured per second
• This means the recording takes up more storage space
• Larger files take longer to upload and stream, which could be an issue for podcast hosting platforms with storage limits
• For speech-only content, 22,050 Hz may be adequate quality, making the larger file unnecessary

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether MP3 or FLAC is the better audio format for distributing music online.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both formats with clear analysis and a reasoned conclusion. QWC: specialist terminology used accurately.
Mid band (4-6): Sound discussion covering both sides.
Lower band (1-3): Basic comparison.
Indicative content:
MP3:
• Very small file sizes due to lossy compression (typically 3–4 MB per song)
• Universally supported on all devices and platforms
• Faster to download and stream, using less bandwidth
• However, some audio quality is permanently lost
FLAC:
• Preserves 100% of the original audio quality using lossless compression
• Preferred by audiophiles who value high-fidelity sound
• Open-source with no licensing fees
• However, file sizes are much larger (10–30 MB per song)
• Requires more bandwidth to stream and more storage to host
• Not supported on all devices, particularly some older hardware
Conclusion: MP3 is better for mass distribution where accessibility matters; FLAC is better for high-quality niche audiences willing to accept larger downloads.

before.content_html:
What Are Moving Image Files?

Moving image files include videos and animations. Whether digital or traditional film, video is fundamentally a series of still images that, when played in sequence at a certain speed, create the appearance of motion. Each individual image is called a frame. Moving image files are used for DVDs, streamed programmes, social media videos, animations, and live footage.

The two key properties that determine the quality of a moving image file are frame rate and resolution. Understanding these properties is essential for choosing the right file format and settings for different distribution methods.

Frame Rate

Frame rate is the speed at which frames are displayed, expressed as frames per second (fps). If a video is captured and played back at 24 fps, that means 24 distinct still images are shown every second. The higher the frame rate, the smoother the motion appears on screen.

Common frame rates include:

24 fps — the standard for cinema and feature films. Gives a slightly “cinematic” look with natural motion blur. 25 fps — the standard for UK television broadcasting (PAL). 30 fps — common for online video, social media content, and US television (NTSC). 60 fps — used for sports broadcasts, gaming, and slow-motion footage. Produces very smooth motion but generates larger file sizes because twice as many frames are captured per second.

Key Fact

Higher frame rates produce smoother video but create larger file sizes. A video at 60 fps contains twice as many frames as the same video at 30 fps, so the file will be approximately twice as large.

Resolution

Resolution describes the total number of pixels on screen. It is expressed as pixel dimensions (width × height). The more pixels, the sharper and more detailed the image. The specification requires you to know five resolution standards:

SD (Standard Definition) — 720 × 576 pixels (PAL) or 720 × 480 pixels (NTSC). The original digital TV standard. Good enough for older TVs, DVD playback, and video sharing at lower quality. Limited detail compared to modern standards.

HD (High Definition) — 1280 × 720 pixels (720p) or 1920 × 1080 pixels (1080p, also called Full HD). Much clearer than SD with significantly more pixels. The standard for most HD broadcasts, streaming services, Blu-ray, and modern TV. 1080p is the most widely used resolution for online video today.

UHD (Ultra High Definition) / 4K — 3840 × 2160 pixels. Four times the pixel count of 1080p Full HD. Used in cinema, some Blu-ray releases, high-end gaming, and premium streaming (Netflix 4K, YouTube 4K). Requires powerful hardware to edit and play back smoothly.

8K — 7680 × 4320 pixels. Sixteen times the pixel count of 1080p. Currently used in very high-end production, visual effects work, and some experimental TV broadcasts. Very few consumers have 8K displays. File sizes are enormous.

SD: 720 × 576 — DVD, older TV broadcasts. HD (720p): 1280 × 720 — some streaming, older broadcasts. Full HD (1080p): 1920 × 1080 — Blu-ray, most streaming, standard TV. 4K/UHD: 3840 × 2160 — cinema, premium streaming, high-end gaming. 8K: 7680 × 4320 — high-end production, visual effects, experimental broadcasts.

Key Fact

Higher resolution means more pixels, sharper images, and better detail — but also much larger file sizes. 4K has four times as many pixels as 1080p Full HD. 8K has sixteen times as many.

Moving Image File Formats

Moving image file formats serve different purposes depending on quality requirements, compatibility, and distribution method. These formats are often described as containers — they package together video data, audio data, and metadata (such as subtitles and chapter markers) into a single file.

MP4 (.mp4) — The most widely used video format. A container format that supports high-quality video with efficient compression. Compatible with virtually all devices, browsers, and platforms. Used by YouTube, social media platforms, and most streaming services. Supports both H.264 and H.265 codecs. Very few limitations — the standard choice for most video distribution.

MOV (.mov) — Apple’s video container format, developed by Apple for QuickTime. Widely used for video files from digital cameras, providing good quality. Well supported on Mac systems and professional editing software. Limitation: not as universally supported as MP4, particularly on some Windows and Android devices.

AVI (.avi) — Audio Video Interleave, developed by Microsoft. An older, typically uncompressed video format that produces very high quality. Often used during video editing before exporting to a compressed format. Limitation: file sizes can be extremely large. Not all devices can play AVI files without installing additional software (codecs).

MPEG / MPG (.mpg) — An older compressed video format using lossy compression for smaller file sizes and faster loading. Used on DVDs and some broadcast systems. Limitation: compression can noticeably lower video quality compared to modern formats like MP4.

MKV (.mkv) — Matroska Video. An open-source container that can hold virtually any combination of video, audio, and subtitle tracks. Popular for high-quality video distribution and media libraries. Limitation: not supported natively by all devices and may require third-party players.

WMV (.wmv) — Windows Media Video. Microsoft’s proprietary format. Produces small files with reasonable quality. Limitation: mainly supported on Windows systems, with limited compatibility on Mac and mobile devices.

GIF (.gif) — Supports short, looping animations with no audio. Limited to 256 colours, so quality is low but file sizes are very small. Widely used for social media reactions, memes, and simple web animations. Not suitable for high-quality video.

SWF (.swf) — Adobe Flash format, previously used for interactive animations and games on websites. Supports lossless compression and interactivity. Largely obsolete since Adobe discontinued Flash Player in 2020. Most modern browsers no longer support SWF files.

WebM (.webm) — An open web media format developed by Google. Uses both lossy and lossless compression. Designed for efficient web video and animation. Supported by most modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Edge). Limitation: not compatible with all devices and older software.

Codecs and Compression

A codec (coder-decoder) is the software that compresses video data for storage and decompresses it for playback. The container (MP4, MOV, AVI) holds the data; the codec determines how that data is compressed.

H.264 (also called AVC) is the most widely used video codec. It provides good quality at relatively small file sizes and is supported on virtually all devices. H.265 (also called HEVC) is the successor to H.264. It achieves similar quality at roughly half the file size, making it ideal for 4K content. However, H.265 requires more powerful hardware to encode and decode.

Key Fact

Rendering is the process of using specialist software to compile edited video, audio, effects, and transitions into a final playable file. It can take significant processing time, especially for high-resolution or effects-heavy projects.

Choosing the Right Format

Format choice depends on the intended distribution method and audience. For web and social media, MP4 with H.264 codec is the standard — widely compatible with small file sizes. For professional editing, AVI or MOV preserves quality during production. For DVD distribution, MPEG format is used. For high-quality archiving or media libraries, MKV can store multiple audio and subtitle tracks in one file.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'frame rate'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• The number of individual frames/still images (1) displayed per second in a video (1)
• Measured in frames per second (fps) (1)
• Accept: how many images are shown per second to create the appearance of motion (2)

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between SD and HD resolution.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• SD (Standard Definition) has a resolution of 720 × 576 pixels (1)
• HD (High Definition) has a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels / 1080p (1)
• HD has significantly more pixels than SD, producing a much sharper, more detailed image (1)
• Accept references to 720p (1280 × 720) as HD.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a higher frame rate for a video.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks (2 per point):
Advantage:
• A higher frame rate produces smoother motion (1), which is important for fast-moving content like sports or gaming where jerky playback would be distracting (1).

Disadvantage:
• A higher frame rate creates a larger file size because more frames are captured each second (1), which means more storage is needed and the video takes longer to upload or stream (1).

practice_questions.text: A school wants to upload a promotional video to its website. Explain why MP4 would be a suitable file format for this purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation linking MP4 properties to the web distribution scenario.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation with some development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points.
Indicative content:
• MP4 uses compression (H.264 codec) to keep file sizes small
• Small file sizes mean the video loads quickly on the website, even on slower internet connections
• MP4 is compatible with virtually all web browsers and devices (desktops, tablets, phones)
• This means all visitors can watch the video regardless of their device or operating system
• MP4 supports high quality video and audio, so the promotional video will look and sound professional
• Streaming platforms and video hosting services universally support MP4

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of distributing a film in 4K resolution compared to Full HD (1080p).
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough discussion of both sides with clear analysis and a reasoned conclusion. QWC: specialist terminology used accurately.
Mid band (4-6): Sound discussion covering both sides.
Lower band (1-3): Basic comparison.
Indicative content:
4K advantages:
• 3840 × 2160 pixels — four times the detail of 1080p
• Much sharper, more detailed image, especially on large screens
• Better for cinema and high-end home viewing
• Increasingly standard on premium streaming platforms
4K disadvantages:
• File sizes are significantly larger, requiring more storage and faster internet for streaming
• Requires powerful hardware to edit and render
• Not all viewers have 4K-capable displays — the extra quality is wasted on HD screens
• Higher bandwidth costs for streaming providers
1080p advantages:
• Smaller file sizes, easier to stream and store
• Universally supported on all modern devices
• Still provides excellent quality for most viewing situations
Conclusion: 4K is best for premium content where quality is paramount; 1080p remains the practical standard for mass distribution.
